title: Longest Substring of One Repeating Character
statement:
You get a string `s` (indexed from 0) and `k` queries, described by a string `queryCharacters` and an integer array `queryIndices`, both of length `k`. Query `i` overwrites the character of `s` at position `queryIndices[i]` with `queryCharacters[i]`. The queries run in order, and each change stays in place for the later ones.

After each query, measure the longest substring of the current `s` made of a single letter repeated (every character in it is the same). Return these `k` lengths as an array, in query order.
constraints: s contains only lowercase English letters
queryCharacters contains only lowercase English letters
signature: int[] longestRepeating(String s, String queryCharacters, int[] queryIndices)
notes:
## Intuition

Rescanning the whole string after every query costs O(n) each, O(n·k) in total: too slow for 10⁵ of each. A single change only matters locally, so keep a segment tree in which every node summarises its range with three numbers: the longest run of one letter starting at its left edge (`prefix`), the longest ending at its right edge (`suffix`), and the longest anywhere inside (`best`). Two neighbouring ranges combine in O(1): a run can only cross the boundary when the letters on both sides of it, `chars[mid]` and `chars[mid + 1]`, are equal. An update then refreshes just the O(log n) nodes above the changed position, and the root's `best` is the answer.

## Approach

1. Copy `s` into `chars` and allocate `prefix`, `suffix` and `best` for 4n nodes.
2. `pull` combines a node from its children. `joins` says whether the boundary letters match. `prefix` is the left child's, extended by the right child's prefix when the left child is one full run and `joins` holds; `suffix` is symmetric. `best` is the larger child best, or the run across the boundary `suffix[left] + prefix[right]` when `joins`.
3. `build` sets every leaf to 1 and pulls each inner node from the bottom up.
4. For each query, write the letter into `chars`, walk `update` down to its leaf and re-pull every node on the way back up, then push `best[1]` into `lengths`.

## Example 1, step by step

`s = "babacc"`. Query 1 makes `chars = "bbbacc"`; on the way up, the node for `bbb` (positions 0..2) sees matching letters across its boundary and gets `best = 3`, which reaches the root: `3`. Query 2 gives `"bbbccc"`: the right half `ccc` now also has `best = 3`, but `b` and `c` meet in the middle, so the root stays `3`. Query 3 gives `"bbbbcc"`: the right half's `prefix` is 1 and `joins` holds at the middle, so `suffix[left] + prefix[right] = 3 + 1 = 4`. The answer is `[3, 3, 4]`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n + k log n): building visits every node once, each query re-pulls one root-to-leaf path.
- Space: O(n) for the tree arrays and `chars`.

## Pitfalls

- A prefix may spill into the right child only when the left child's prefix covers its whole range (`mid - lo + 1`); likewise for suffixes and `hi - mid`.
- Compare the letters at `mid` and `mid + 1` after writing the new letter into `chars`, or the merge uses stale data.
- A query may write the letter that is already there; the answer must simply stay the same.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `chars` | the current letters of `s` |
| `prefix[node]` | longest one-letter run starting at the node's left edge |
| `suffix[node]` | longest one-letter run ending at the node's right edge |
| `best[node]` | longest one-letter run inside the node's range |
| `lo`, `hi`, `mid` | the node's range and its split point |
| `joins` | whether the two halves' boundary letters are equal |
| `lengths` | the answer after each query |
